text:
Good video.  To explain decoupling for high speed devices with lots of simultaneous switching noise (like FPGAs), inductance plays a big part. Notice: AC takes the path of least inductance, so at very high noise frequencies, any small inductance between the capacitors and noise generating device can render the capacitors less effective or useless. Even the ground/power planes have some inductance and the leads on the device and capacitors have even a bit more inductance.  On a breadboard, it is difficult to keep the leads short and close to the device. Even a millimeter of lead length can add enough inductance so Very High Frequency (VHF)  components of the noise are not decoupled. This is why Surface Mount Technology (SMT) capacitors and devices are now used rather than through-hole components, even the length of the trace through the holes and vias add inductance.  This is why decoupling capacitors are placed directly under components right next to power pins with many redundant vias to reduce the inductance. Also, capacitors with a low Effective Series Resistance (ESR) have lower internal inductance and thus can decouple a wider bandwidth of noise. At this point each group of capacitors and power pin is a tiny localized Ultra High Frequency (UHF) Resistor Capacitor Inductor (RCL) circuit - the symbol L is used for inductance. Dr. Howard Johnson has awesome seminars on this. At today's billions of transitors switching at many GHz rates, these tiny dimensions become critical and you can't even look at a millimeter of Copper clad from a DC perspective anymore, you have to consider the high frequency AC aspects more and more - it becomes all very mechanically sensitive at this point.  This is why it is common to have 3 decoupling capacitors for every power pin. A 0.01uf, a 0.1uf, and a 1uf, all SMT devices, all very close to the power pins with the smaller values closest to the power pins. This gives a wide band of decoupling from UHF down to Medium Frequencies (MF). For circuits that consume a lot of power and have Low Frequecy (LF) and Very Low Frequency (VLF) noise down to DC, larger 10uf to 100uf capacitors are required all over the board but these can be a bit further from the power pins due to inductance has less effect on lower frequencies as you approach DC. This creates islands of "hold up voltage" or "power reservoirs" all over the board - with the inductance between the circuits keeping the islands isolated at UHF even though there is a large DC path between them.

In your example, even though it was a breadboard and you were using leaded components (as an example), you put the larger capacitor close to the 555 Timer.  In your case it didn't really matter on a breadboard.  People need to remember this video was a good demo, but you need to get into the habit of placing the smaller capacitor values closest to the power pins, with virtally no leads and no wires (mounted on the power/ground planes directly with SMT devices with low ESR and lots of Vias).

That jumper wire you made from the Regulator to the 555 Timer has a lot of relative inductance, so as the 555 Timer output switches, the change in current (AC) that is supplying the Timer from the Regulator is partially blocked by that inductance and thus the circuits inside the Timer don't have enough local power reserves to recover properly.

Remember:
Capacitors block DC and pass AC, while Inductors pass DC and block AC.
Even a tiny piece of of wire/lead/via/through-hole has significant inductance at UHF, and even DC planes have some inductance.

text: @ddognine  Thanks for the comment. Not only have I been doing this since high school electronics in 1977, I teach it in my free Summer STEM class. I first learned about decoupling in high school electronics. I was building a multi stage counter circuit with 74 series TTL chips. It was counting wrong at times, my teacher showed me how to look for noise on the o-scope and to put in decoupling caps next to each chip. It fixed the problem.  If you ever have a chance to attend any of Dr. Howard Johnson's seminars on signal integrity, take them. He sacles things up 10x so you can see the mechanics of it all and to lower the bandwidth on effects for discussion and examination. I once asked him if he could do a seminar on Ball Grid Array (BGA) inductance and decoupling. He did, I think he has a video on it. These days, FPGA pins are mounted underneath the chip with a matrix of tiny solder balls, when heated, they melt and make 100's of connections between the chip and board in seconds. The thing is, FPGAs (and many CPUs) get so hot you have to bond a thin aluminum plate to the bottom of the board as a heat sink. So you can't probe any pins... you have to use JTAG to test the connections or use JTAG to monitor the signals. I made a JTAG tool that allowed us to monitor signals between non JTAG devices and some JTAG-able FPGAs in real time, we had to slow down the signals but it gave a graphic display on the toggling of the pins (balls) to see if any are stuck/shorted/open. I designed that tool back in 2001, I hear they still use it on the F-22 project.  We had an in-house subject matter expert on signal integrity, and I was the JTAG subject matter expert. We had regular "lunch-n-learn" seminars at work... so many companies forget that we each have our areas of expertise and sharing these ideas at lunch (company buys us lunch) is a great way for a company to really move ahead down the high tech road.  I have to give credit to one of my mentors when I was a young pup engineer. Harry Clayton showed me to select capacitors that had the lowest ESR and the shortest leads to reduce the inductance and widen the capacitor's filtering bandwidth for better and higher frequency decoupling. The guy had an IQ of about 200, I was dirt compared to him at a mere 165 IQ, so he took me under his wing... a great guy, great engineer, and great beer homebrewer.

text:
Note that if your device has screw terminals or anything else that may induce mechanical stress, do not place ceramic SMD caps directly at the terminals. Mechanical stress can make cracks form in between the layers and that results in a dead short. With enough input current, the capacitor will vaporize itself and traces in its vicinity right through the entire PCB. If you wanna see what that looks like, EEVblog did a video on that.
https://youtu.be/Q2rvAoO-MIA
author: @PunakiviAddikti

text: @PunakiviAddikti  Good point. But if you are using equipment that has screw terminals that is not a good place for any "decoupling" capacitors nearby due to the high inductance of the screw terminal post and its terminal block, so small SMT caps are useless there anyway. In those cases, very large decoupling capacitors are used, these we call "Bus Caps" because they don't do any decoupling but create local "reservoirs" of power to reduce power rail (bus) sag due to high current transients... they are basically local hold up capacitors. Through hole devices are ok there because power is the issue, not noise.  I once designed a test backplane for a folded 4-section PC board (4 PCBs interconnected with flex cables and folded up into one module). There were 24 Xilinx Virtex-II FPGAs running at 50MHz on that board.  That board really sucked up power. I had to use many "Screw to 10 pin DIP Terminals" that were press fit into the backplane's heavily plated PCB though holes. I had about 50 100uF decoupling caps all over the backplane as bus caps. These FPGAs use 3.3V I/O and, if I recall, 1.5V logic. I had to parallel two HP 50 Amp supplies together and use 10AWG twisted pair power leads from the supplies to the Backplane for the 1.5 Volts alone. 135 Watts just for the internal logic.  Talk about in-rush current!

See my other response on this. I use very large value though hole "bus caps" near those terminals, not small SMT "decoupling caps" because the high inductance of the Terminal Adapters make low inductive decoupling caps nearby useless.  The designers of the board in that video obviously did not fully understand decoupling and inductance, those tiny (lower value) caps near those Terminal Adapters are doing virtually nothing. author: @SheikhN-bible-syndrome

text: @SheikhN-bible-syndrome  If the amplifer is in the audio range and the noise is in that range too, then a few millimeters of lead between the cap and the device won't make much difference. But, if you get into the Giga Hz, then 1 millimeter starts to become a significant inductance that will limit the bandwidth of the to cap to filter out noise. The lead and the cap start to act as a tuned tank circuit. This is why high frequency AC travels along the surface of a wire (skin effect)... if you can imagine that the cross section of a wire is in fact an infinite series of concentric circles of copper (an infinite series of inductors) with the least inductance being the outer surface where the inductance is least, and the center of the wire where the tighter radius inductance is the most... since AC travels along the path of least inductance, the AC electrons travel more along the surface of the wire. This is also why wires are rated to carry more DC current than AC. So when the frequecy goes up, inductance and capacitance start to factor in to everything.

text: All the decoupling capacitors do is to compensate for your PDN’s (power delivery network) inductance. They essentially act as Columb buckets of charge to handle local power demand. The noise you see at the 7805 regulator’s input is generated by your bench’s switching power supply along with the long connection leads. If you improve your PDN ‘s design & layout you may find that the decoupling capacitors aren’t needed at all. The measurement of power supply noise is also greatly affected by probing technique. It is best to have the probe’s signal and signal return’s (i.e.) as close together & as short as possible as not to introduce unwanted impedance mismatch which’ll create false noise readings.

text: It says right there in the datasheet for this LINEAR regulator, that a capacitor is required on the input for STABILITY. Without it, the regulating feedback amplifier inside the regulator becomes unstable. That is, any small variations in the INPUT voltage cause the feedback amplifier to unintentionally react, causing a change in output voltage and therefore load current that causes the the input voltage to change even more due to the source impedance (lead inductance). This is positive feedback, and it causes the oscillation that you see. This is NOT noise, it is instability. Adding the input capacitor makes the input voltage much less sensitive to rapid changes in load current, enough that any unintentional reaction by the regulator does not change the current enough to make things worse. It's all about how fast the input voltage changes in response to changes in output voltage and corresponding load current. Too fast and the regulator's negative feedback can't compensate for the positive feedback cause by the amplifiers response to fast input voltage changes. The instability gets worse, as you have shown, when the load is greater, since the current changes more with the output voltage, thus effecting the input voltage more. The datasheet notes that the input capacitor is only required if the regulator is far from the filter capacitors of the supply, as they would do the same job, but with long leads, the inductance of these leads is too much and the input voltage becomes more sensitive to the current changes.

text:
Many regulators, especially some of the older "low dropout voltage" types absolutely must have a fairly substantial amount of capacitance at their output for stability. The ancient 7800 series are pretty tolerant, but dynamic performance is still improved with some capacitance at the output.

Edit: Some of the older LDO regulators were also very fussy about the equivalent series resistance (ESR) of the cap put across their output. An acceptable range would be specified. If the ESR were too low or too high the performance would be compromised. Most newer types will tolerate "zero" ESR.

text: The video looks very nice, the explanations are severely oversimplified at best and completely wrong at worst. The Wikipedia page you show at 0:26 clearly mentions what noise is (random fluctuations); the rest of the video uses the word noise where the actual phenomena are oscillation and coupling. You don't show the effect of loading on the output on your lab supply, which has a significant impact on the performance of the 7805 as it will pass frequencies over a few hundred kHz straight through. The input capacitor C1 affects regulator stability (->oscillation), not noise. You very briefly mention breadboard being "not ideal" -- it's fairly common to get > 1Ohm contact resistance on most breadboards, which strongly impacts your measurements. The output stage of the old school 555 is well known to have shoot through, which makes switching transients pretty bad in circuits of these. Finally: where do you decouple *to*? What is the role of the load in all of this?

text:
High frequency performance of electrolytic capacitors is generally significantly poorer than that of ceramic capacitors simply because of the physical construction. Ceramic capacitor high frequency performance is generally very good, but, at least historically, large-value ceramic caps have been physically large and quite expensive. Using a small ceramic in parallel with an electrolytic yields pretty good performance across a wide frequency range.

You can now get ceramic capacitors of 10 µF or more at low cost and in small packages, at least as surface mount parts. I very strongly recommend against any of the Zxx or Yxx types. They are small and cheap, but many have extraordinarily large negative voltage coefficient of capacitance. A 10 V part operated at 5 V may have only half or less of its nominal capacitance. X7R or X5R much less awful.

Sometimes with just a ceramic capacitor you can get into a situation where the capacitor resonates with the stray inductance in the circuit and you can actually make things worse, though this is relatively rare. Electrolytics at high frequency may look like a reasonably good capacitor in series with a resistance. That resistance can "spoil the Q" of the circuit and damp resonance. Solid tantalum caps are an alternative, better than aluminum electrolytics and not quite as good as ceramics at high frequencies. They are quite expensive these days. Tantalums are intolerant of overvoltage and tend to fail short-circuit.

text:
Measuring noise with an oscilloscope can be very daunting. I've spent many hours trying to determine whether noise on a scope screen was real or not. I've done a lot of biggish SMPS design, with switching of  about 400 V and currents of many amperes, slewing in a few tens of nanoseconds. Pickup on the probe ground lead was very rarely an issue. Inductance of that lead is another matter.

One of the issues is that as soon as you connect the scope ground to the circuit under test you MAY introduce a ground loop. You may essentially connect an antenna (the ground of the scope itself; less of a problem with small digital scopes than big metal-cases scopes of years gone by) to ground, so you make a path that didn't exist without the scope.

Differential probes can be a big help and there are some that are fairly reasonably priced these days, at least up to about 100 MHz. I haven't used any of them, so I don't know how good they are.

A resonant circuit is formed between the probe tip capacitance and the probe's ground lead. That can make things appear much worse than they are. FET probes have merit here, but decent ones cost a lot more than the average hobbyist's oscilloscope.

text:
The reason they don't integrate bypass capacitors into 555 timer ICs is primarily due to cost, flexibility, and design considerations..

Cost: Adding bypass capacitors within the IC would increase manufacturing costs. Since bypass capacitors are relatively inexpensive components, it's more cost-effective to place them externally on the PCB (Printed Circuit Board) instead of integrating them directly into the IC.
Flexibility: The value of bypass capacitors depends on the specific application and its requirements. Different applications may need different capacitance values for optimal performance. By keeping the bypass capacitors external, designers can easily select and customize the appropriate capacitance values based on their specific needs.
Design considerations: Integrated circuits are designed to be versatile and adaptable to a wide range of applications. By keeping bypass capacitors external, the IC can be used in various circuit configurations without imposing specific capacitor values or configurations on the designer. This allows for greater flexibility in circuit design and application.
Additionally, external bypass capacitors offer benefits such as easier troubleshooting, modification or upgrading of circuits, and the ability to share capacitors among multiple ICs or components.

While it may seem convenient and proactive to integrate bypass capacitors into ICs, the considerations mentioned above, along with the desire for versatility and cost-effectiveness, have led to the prevailing practice of using external bypass capacitors in most circuit designs, including those involving the 555 timer IC.

text:
These capacitors are not decoupling capacitors. Decoupling capacitors eliminate dc voltages from previous or following stage of circuit modules. Your capacitors do the opposite thing. They form high pass filters grounding high frequency noise from power supply lines, inputs or outputs of circuit modules. Capacitors from power supply lines to ground furthermore form charge buffers, which suppress voltage break downs due to short time higher current requirements of circuit modules.

These buffer capacitors are especially needed in the case of the NE555 timer application because it has no means to suppress shot througs in its output stage. So it uses 200 up to 500 mA for 40 to 100 ns which cannot propagate along the power supply lines to the device because of its inductance. So a voltage regulator cannot react on them. So it only can be covered by the charge of a capacitor immediately located at the power pins of the timer IC.to keep the inductance of the current path low (in the nH range).
